strengths: FLEG addresses a useful computer vision problem: jointly reconstructing appearance and language-aligned 3D representations from unposed images with variable view counts. Combining these capabilities in one feed-forward model has practical value.

The reported improvements are substantial. In Table 1, two-view FLEG achieves 47.12 mIoU and 24.20 PSNR, versus 38.48 and 22.79 for Uni3R, and maintains competitive performance through 32 views despite training with at most 14.

The proposed components form a coherent pipeline: teacher-based geometry supervision, coverage-based target selection, instance-level semantic learning, and separate geometric and semantic Gaussian densities.

Table 3 provides encouraging evidence for instance contrastive learning and sparsification: removing the instance loss reduces mIoU from 44.58 to 39.01, while sparsification reduces semantic embeddings from 6.4M to 2.6M without sacrificing segmentation accuracy. Reported reconstruction times of 1.89–3.20 seconds also suggest a substantial advantage over per-scene optimization.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish generalization. InstanceMV-14K includes ScanNet and ScanNet++, which also supply the evaluation data, but the manuscript does not identify training/test scene splits or explain how overlap is excluded. Evaluation scene counts, context/target sampling, query vocabularies, and camera alignment for novel-view rendering are also missing. This is an unresolved validity concern, not evidence that leakage occurred.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The multi-view adaptation of LSM and Uni3R is described only as DUSt3R-style post-processing, despite dramatic degradation with additional views. Training-data exposure, checkpoint selection, and camera inputs are not sufficiently documented. Several directly relevant cited semantic feed-forward methods are absent, and there is no controlled comparison using the same VGGT backbone and training data to isolate FLEG's contributions.

The ablations do not establish several central claims. Removing all geometric distillation does not isolate the proposed novel-view selection mechanism. There are no ablations of InstanceMV-14K's added data, multi-view feature aggregation, or isotropic versus anisotropic semantic Gaussians. Consequently, gains cannot be confidently attributed to the proposed algorithms rather than the stronger backbone and expanded supervision.

Results require reconciliation: Tables 1 and 2 report different FLEG scores for apparently the same ScanNet view settings—for example, 16-view mIoU is 47.59 versus 44.69—without explaining a protocol difference. The manuscript also does not clarify whether evaluation targets remain fixed across view counts, limiting interpretation of the reported scaling trends.

Important implementation details and ambiguities hinder reproduction. Section 3.4 specifies a smaller semantic voxel size while claiming coarser, sparser aggregation; Eq. (6) uses F, previously defined as the target feature, without clearly identifying the trainable features receiving gradients. These may be correctable notation issues, but voxel sizes, coverage threshold, feature dimensions, contrastive temperature, training duration, and hardware are also unspecified.

Several claims exceed the supplied evidence. '3D-annotation-free' needs qualification because ScanNet/ScanNet++ masks are projected from 3D annotations and geometry supervision comes from pretrained VGGT. Generalization evidence is confined to indoor scan datasets, geometric accuracy is not directly evaluated, and editing is illustrated rather than systematically assessed. Reduced Gaussian counts alone do not establish memory or rendering-speed savings; hardware-controlled measurements are needed for the efficiency claims.

strengths: FLEG addresses a useful computer-vision problem: reconstructing geometry, appearance, and language-aligned semantics from unposed images using one feed-forward model across different view counts. Combining this functionality without an external semantic model at inference has practical value.

The reported improvements are substantial. On ScanNet with two views, FLEG achieves 47.12 mIoU and 24.20 dB PSNR, versus 38.48 and 22.79 for Uni3R. Table 1 also reports relatively stable performance through 32 views, exceeding the maximum of 14 views used during training.

Separating geometric and semantic Gaussian densities is a sensible design. Table 3 reports a reduction from 6.4M to 2.6M semantic embeddings while retaining segmentation quality, and removing the instance loss reduces mIoU from 44.58 to 39.01. These results provide preliminary support for both components.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish generalization. InstanceMV-14K includes ScanNet and ScanNet++, which also supply the evaluation data, but the manuscript does not identify training/test scene splits, evaluated scene counts, or exclusion procedures. This does not establish leakage, but prevents verifying scene-disjoint evaluation. Context/target frame sampling, query vocabularies, segmentation thresholds, and alignment of predicted coordinates with evaluation cameras are also unclear.

Baseline handling materially affects the central comparison. Section 4.3 describes adapting fixed-view methods through DUSt3R-style post-processing without specifying pairing, alignment, Gaussian fusion, or camera inputs. Uni3R's PSNR drops from 22.79 with two views to 10.55 with 32 views; without validating the adaptation, this cannot confidently be attributed to an inherent limitation of prior work. Several closely related semantic feed-forward methods discussed in the paper are not evaluated, and there is no controlled VGGT/AnySplat-based semantic baseline to separate the proposed mechanisms from backbone and training-data advantages.

The ablations do not isolate several principal contributions. Removing geometric distillation demonstrates its importance, but does not test coverage-based novel-view selection against input-view-only or randomly selected target supervision. There are no isolated studies of multi-view feature aggregation, added Internet-video data, dataset scale, or isotropic versus anisotropic semantic Gaussians. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which proposed innovations explain the gains over an otherwise comparable system.

Reported results and efficiency claims need clarification. FLEG's ScanNet scores differ between Tables 1 and 2 at the same view counts: for 16 views, mIoU is 47.59 versus 44.69; for 32 views, mAcc is 74.28 versus 79.52. Different evaluation subsets could explain this, but none are specified. The reported 1.89–3.20 second reconstruction times lack hardware and timing boundaries; peak memory, rendering speed, and measured sparsification speedups are absent. These omissions particularly weaken the real-time and computational-efficiency claims.

Several implementation details impede reproducibility: training duration and batch size, coverage threshold, voxel sizes, feature dimensions, CLIP configuration, contrastive temperature, and pixel sampling are unspecified. Equation 6 uses F, previously defined as the target feature map, leaving the trainable feature source ambiguous. Section 3.4 also describes obtaining fewer semantic Gaussians with a smaller voxel size, contrary to the usual voxel-count relationship. These may be correctable exposition errors, but concern central operations.

The scope of several claims exceeds the evidence. '3D-annotation-free' needs qualification because ScanNet/ScanNet++ instance masks are projected from existing 3D annotations and geometry supervision comes from pretrained VGGT. The demonstrated contribution is avoiding direct geometric ground-truth supervision during this training stage. Likewise, evaluation on indoor datasets with 2–32 views supports flexibility within that range, rather than unrestricted 'any views' generalization. As an Algorithms/General submission, the promising integration is outweighed by unresolved validation and attribution concerns.

strengths: FLEG addresses a valuable computer-vision problem: reconstructing renderable, language-embedded 3D scenes from unposed, uncalibrated images with variable input counts. Jointly supporting novel-view synthesis and open-vocabulary queries without a semantic model at inference offers practical value.

The method integrates several sensible components: VGGT-based geometric supervision, coverage-based target-view selection, instance-guided semantic learning, and separate geometric and semantic Gaussian densities. The semantic sparsification is particularly relevant to the memory overhead of language features.

The reported results are promising. In Table 1, FLEG achieves 47.12 mIoU and 24.20 dB PSNR with two views, compared with 38.48 and 22.79 for Uni3R. Performance remains relatively stable through 32 views, despite training with at most 14 input views.

Table 3 provides useful evidence for instance supervision and sparsification: removing the instance loss reduces mIoU from 44.58 to 39.01, while sparsification reduces semantic embeddings from 6.4M to 2.6M without sacrificing reported accuracy. Table 2 also suggests a substantial reconstruction-time advantage over per-scene optimization.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol is insufficiently specified to establish held-out generalization. InstanceMV-14K includes ScanNet and ScanNet++, which also supply the evaluation data, but the manuscript gives no scene splits, exclusion procedure, evaluation-set sizes, or detailed context/target sampling protocol. This does not establish leakage, but leaves its prevention unverifiable. Moreover, FLEG's ScanNet results differ between Tables 1 and 2 at the same view counts—for example, 16-view mIoU is 47.59 versus 44.69—without explaining whether different scenes or protocols are used.

The comparisons do not adequately isolate the proposed contribution from backbone and training-data advantages. FLEG uses an approximately 1B-parameter VGGT-based model and a newly assembled large dataset, while the main feed-forward comparisons use DUSt3R-based methods. Their dense-view adaptation is described only as post-processing following DUSt3R, despite severe degradation that materially drives the claimed advantage. A controlled VGGT/AnySplat-based semantic baseline, together with explicit baseline training and adaptation details, would substantially strengthen the case. Several closely related semantic feed-forward methods discussed in the paper are also not evaluated.

The ablations leave central claims untested. Removing all geometric distillation demonstrates reliance on geometric supervision, but does not isolate the proposed coverage-based novel-view selection. There are no separate tests of multi-view feature aggregation, the contribution of Internet-video training data, or isotropic semantic covariance approximation. Consequently, the evidence does not yet establish which proposed innovations explain the gains beyond the pretrained foundation model and expanded training set.

Important implementation details are missing or ambiguous: training duration and batch size, CLIP configuration and feature dimensions, coverage threshold, voxel sizes, contrastive temperature, and alignment of teacher geometry with predictions from a context subset. Equation 6 uses F, previously defined as the target feature map, leaving unclear which predicted features receive the contrastive gradient. Section 3.4 also describes a smaller semantic voxel size as producing greater sparsity, contrary to the usual effect of voxel size. These ambiguities hinder reproduction, although the notation and voxel-size wording may be correctable presentation errors.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete. Reconstruction timings lack hardware and measurement details; there are no peak-memory measurements, feed-forward baseline timings, or direct runtime/memory ablations for hierarchical sparsification. Because sparsification follows dense prediction and transformer processing, fewer retained semantic Gaussians alone does not establish reduced peak inference memory. The reported seconds-per-scene timings support fast reconstruction, but not the broader real-time application claims.

The '3D-annotation-free' claim needs qualification: the framework uses a pretrained geometry teacher, and the actual training dataset includes masks projected from annotated 3D scans. This is a useful reduction in additional annotation requirements, but the experiments do not demonstrate independence from 3D-derived supervision. Overall, the promising integration and reported gains are outweighed by unresolved evaluation and attribution concerns under an Algorithms/General assessment.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, FLEG addresses a useful computer-vision problem: reconstructing renderable, language-aligned 3D scenes from variable numbers of unposed images. Combining flexible inputs with compact semantic Gaussians provides practical value beyond improving a single benchmark.

The compact representation is supported by convincing within-model comparisons. Table 3 reduces embeddings from 2.012M to 73.89K and reported embedding storage from 491.3 MB to 18.04 MB, while maintaining mIoU (46.69 versus 46.87). The supplementary sparsity sweep further supports a favorable storage–accuracy tradeoff.

Results are consistently strong on ScanNet and ScanNet++. Even with equal two-view inputs, FLEG improves over Uni3R on ScanNet++ from 39.54 to 46.61 mIoU and from 24.95 to 28.14 dB PSNR, so its advantages cannot be attributed solely to receiving more images.

The ablations support important components: removing instance contrast reduces mIoU from 46.87 to 40.22, while removing novel-view distillation reduces PSNR from 26.66 to 24.77. Supplementary pose, depth, and unseen-Replica evaluations broaden the evidence beyond the main tasks.

The manuscript generally explains the architecture and aggregation equations clearly, credits its foundation models and datasets, and explicitly acknowledges indoor-only generalization, teacher dependence, and limitations at very large view counts.
weaknesses: The novel-view distillation procedure has a consequential ambiguity. Only context images enter the student, yet Appendix A states that all geometric distillation terms—including camera and depth-head terms—are computed on novel views. It is unclear how student camera/depth-head predictions for withheld images are obtained. The teacher–student coordinate and scale alignment during training also needs an explicit description.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the coverage threshold, geometric voxel size, contrastive temperature and sampling settings, feature-decoder specification, and optimization schedule are not supplied. The semantic voxel default is also inconsistent: Figure 5 labels 0.16, whereas the accompanying text states 0.016. These settings directly affect the central sparsity and distillation results.

Efficiency evidence establishes embedding compression, but not the broader real-time deployment claims. No inference latency, peak GPU memory, rendering throughput, or view-count scaling measurements are reported for the approximately 1B-parameter model. Full storage accounting should include the additional semantic Gaussian geometry and decoder, beyond embedding arrays.

The experimental comparisons leave attribution gaps. Above two views, LSM and Uni3R receive only the nearest image pair, a transparently explained but limited comparison against genuinely multi-view semantic reconstruction. Table 2 uses an unspecified validation subset, without scene counts or identifiers. A controlled comparison using the same semantic teacher would also help separate architectural gains from differences in semantic supervision.

The originality and necessity of specific DGLE choices need stronger evidence. Semantic sparsity and decoupling are already acknowledged in DF-3DGS, but the distinction is discussed only briefly. Comparisons against simple coarse semantic pooling and anisotropic moment matching would clarify the benefit of the proposed isotropic construction. Overall, the empirical gains support a slight preference for acceptance, but methodological clarity and efficiency validation prevent a stronger recommendation.

strengths: Assessed as Algorithms/General, FLEG addresses a useful computer-vision problem: reconstructing renderable, language-aligned 3D scenes from a variable number of unposed images. Combining flexible inputs with a compact semantic representation has practical value.

The compact representation is supported by a meaningful controlled comparison. Table 3 reduces embeddings from 2.012M to 73.89K and embedding storage from 491.3 MB to 18.04 MB, while retaining similar segmentation quality: 46.87 versus 46.69 mIoU. The supplementary sparsity sweep further supports this tradeoff.

Results are consistently strong on the main datasets. Even with matched two-view inputs, FLEG exceeds LSM and Uni3R in segmentation and rendering on both ScanNet++ and ScanNet, and exceeds AnySplat in rendering. Thus, the improvements cannot be explained solely by access to more input views.

The ablations support important components: removing instance contrastive learning reduces mIoU from 46.87 to 40.22, and removing novel-view distillation reduces PSNR from 26.66 to 24.77. Supplementary Replica experiments provide useful evidence of cross-dataset semantic generalization, alongside camera and depth evaluations.

The manuscript acknowledges dependence on VGGT, indoor-domain training, and memory limitations at large view counts. Overall, the demonstrated semantic accuracy and storage savings support a slight preference for acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The novel-view supervision pipeline needs a more precise account. The student receives only context images, yet Appendix A states that all geometric distillation terms, including camera supervision, are computed on novel views. It is unclear how student camera predictions for withheld images are obtained. Likewise, the inference statement following Eq. (4) does not explain how arbitrary target-camera poses are supplied or estimated. These ambiguities affect reproducibility and interpretation of the pose-free claim.

Originality of the compact representation is insufficiently distinguished from related work. The paper explicitly acknowledges semantic sparsity in DF-3DGS, while DGLE combines voxel aggregation, moment matching, and isotropic approximation. A clearer technical comparison with prior decoupled feature representations, plus controlled comparisons against simpler coarse aggregation and anisotropic fusion, would establish which design choices provide the benefit.

The efficiency evidence concerns stored embeddings rather than end-to-end efficiency. No inference latency, peak GPU memory, semantic rendering throughput, or total asset storage is reported. DGLE still starts from dense predicted embeddings, adds separate Gaussian geometry, and uses an approximately 1B-parameter network. Consequently, the storage reduction does not establish the broader claims about scalable or real-time deployment.

Comparison coverage has limitations. Beyond two views, LSM and Uni3R receive only the two nearest images, whereas FLEG receives all available inputs. This is a disclosed, reasonable checkpoint-based comparison, but it does not isolate architectural quality from input availability. Table 2 also uses an unspecified validation subset without scene counts, identifiers, or sufficient per-scene optimization details, weakening the reproducibility of its particularly large gains.

Several consequential implementation details are missing or inconsistent: the coverage threshold, geometric voxel size, contrastive temperature and sampling procedure, embedding/decoder configuration, and optimizer schedule are not adequately specified. Figure 5 marks the default semantic voxel size as 0.16, whereas the accompanying text states 0.016; this factor-of-ten discrepancy directly affects reproduction of the central compression result.

Some conclusions exceed the evidence. Replica rendering does not consistently outperform AnySplat, and Table 2 does not show universal metric superiority. The evaluation changes target views with input count, so it does not establish how adding observations improves reconstruction for fixed targets. Instance discrimination and 3D editing also receive substantially less direct evaluation than semantic segmentation and novel-view rendering.

strengths: FLEG makes a useful Algorithms/General contribution by combining pose-free, variable-view Gaussian reconstruction with compact language-aligned semantics. The unified model addresses a practical limitation of existing two-view semantic reconstruction methods.

The compact semantic representation is convincingly supported by Table 3: embedding count drops from 2.012M to 73.89K and reported embedding storage from 491.3 MB to 18.04 MB, while mIoU remains comparable (46.69 versus 46.87). The supplementary sparsity sweep further supports this tradeoff.

Results are consistently strong across ScanNet++ and ScanNet. Even in the matched two-view setting, FLEG improves substantially over LSM and Uni3R in both semantic segmentation and novel-view synthesis, so the gains cannot be explained solely by access to more input images.

The main training components have meaningful ablation support. Removing instance-guided contrastive learning reduces mIoU from 46.87 to 40.22; removing novel-view distillation reduces PSNR from 26.66 to 24.77. These results substantiate the proposed semantic and geometric supervision.

The supplementary material strengthens the evidence with unseen-Replica evaluation, camera-pose and depth comparisons, and explicit discussion of indoor generalization and memory limitations. Overall, the demonstrated semantic accuracy and representation savings support acceptance.
weaknesses: Practical efficiency is incompletely evaluated. Despite emphasizing real-time applications and scalable reconstruction, the paper reports no inference latency, peak GPU memory, or rendering throughput versus input-view count. Embedding-storage savings alone do not establish deployment efficiency for a roughly one-billion-parameter model; total asset storage, including the additional semantic Gaussian parameters, should also be reported.

The novelty of semantic decoupling needs sharper positioning against DF-3DGS, which the paper explicitly acknowledges as exploring semantic sparsity. Table 3 establishes the benefit over dense embeddings, but does not isolate the value of moment-matched isotropic Gaussians relative to simpler coarse-voxel aggregation or retaining anisotropic covariances.

Several details needed for reproduction are missing or ambiguous: the coverage threshold, geometric voxel size, embedding dimension, contrastive temperature, and optimizer schedule are not specified. Figure 5 labels the default semantic voxel size as 0.16, whereas the accompanying text states 0.016. The novel-view camera supervision also needs clarification because the student receives only context images, yet Appendix A says all geometric distillation terms are computed on novel views.

The evaluation has limits that should qualify the broad superiority claims. At higher view counts, LSM and Uni3R still receive only the two nearest views, so those comparisons measure available-system capability rather than matched multi-view processing. Table 2 uses an unspecified validation subset without reporting its size or scene identities, making its large gains harder to assess.

The evidence supports indoor semantic reconstruction more strongly than the full range of advertised capabilities. Three-dimensional editing is largely illustrative, and semantic accuracy is measured through rendered views rather than direct 3D consistency or instance-level discrimination. Replica results also show that novel-view rendering does not uniformly outperform AnySplat.
